title: Can VLMs Diagnose and Recover from VLA Manipulation Faults?
claim: A benchmark organizes failures into a hierarchy of types and severity levels, exposing a gap between human and model diagnosis.
layout: Dense mosaic: central wheel, severity levels left, judger panels right, three task cards below
description: A dense, multi-region figure built around a circular wheel at the center labeled VLA-FixBench-6K. The wheel is split into three colored sectors: Perception (gray), Planning (blue) and Control (orange). Each sector holds small robot scene thumbnails labeled with fault types such as Blur, Distortion, Pose error, Collision, Delay and Overshooting. On the left, three stacked cards for Level-1, Level-2 and Level-3 severity show robot photos with green checks and red crosses for Approach, Grasp and Transport. On the right, a Human Judger System panel (blue, with an upward success-rate arrow) sits above a VLM Judger System panel (red, with a downward arrow). Between them is the question 'What abilities are missing in VLMs compared to humans?'. Along the bottom, three cards cover Failure, Temporal Localization and Spatial Deviation Understanding. Each pairs a task example with a question mark prompt.
caption: Overview of VLA-FixBench, Center: Hierarchical failure types in Perception, Planning, and Control. Left: Severity
abstract: Existing VLA models frequently fail in robotic manipulation tasks, with poorly structured fault types that often require expert diagnosis. While VLMs offer strong explanatory capabilities, their effectiveness in assisting VLAs is limited by their unclear role in diagnostics and inadequate collaboration mechanisms. To address this, we introduce VLA-FixBench, a fault evaluation dataset that spans perception, planning, and control failures, and provides annotations for task stages, fault types, and spatiotemporal repair strategies. We further propose FaultEval, a static-to-dynamic-to-real evaluation framework that benchmarks 20 VLMs across multiple fault-related dimensions. Building on these insights, we design a VLM–VLA collaboration mechanism that localizes spatiotemporal deviations and rolls back task execution to enable targeted recovery. Experiments show that FaultEval reliably characterizes VLM-based closed-loop diagnosis and repair. The upper-bound analysis using human expert intervention shows that an idealized feedback loop can improve task success rates by 13\% on LIBERO and 35\% on real-world robots. Our code, benchmark, and project page will be publicly released at: https://kakigo.github.io/VLA-FixBench/
